cd-mt-tom-park.st: On July 4th, 1906, the Swedish Lutherans held their celebration in "the grove adjoining Mount Tom". People took the interurban to the North Side cemetery and walked from there (Eau Claire Leader, 1 Jul 1906, p. 13). So the picnic grove was on the cemetery side of the hill, and that side is worth checking along with the summit.
src: Eau Claire Leader, 1 Jul 1906, p. 13 (newspapers.com image 239382600)

d-carson-park.st: Before it was Carson Park, the land inside the Half Moon Lake horseshoe seems to have been the resort the papers called "Horseshoe Island". In 1903 the Leader called it a "favorite summer resort for the people of this city", with a grand concert there while "Half Moon Lake is literally covered with boats" (Eau Claire Leader, 9 Aug 1903, p. 6). In 1905 the Boot and Shoe Workers union held the season's first open-air ball there (Leader, 14 Jun 1905, p. 6). On July 4th, 1906, there was all-day dancing in the island pavilion, log-rolling, a 250-yard swim, canoe races and fireworks (Leader, 1 Jul 1906, p. 13). People came by launch and rowboat. On the 1902 Leader county map the lake almost rings this land (then Daniel Shaw Lumber Co., 148.9 acres), joined to the mainland only by a narrow neck at the south end. That makes it the likely "island", though the papers don't say so outright. Where the pavilion stood isn't known yet; the old boat landings on the island shore are the place to start.
